flawed_step: Step 4: the claim that at least one of the listed single interchanges must succeed. The Kempe case, where the 1-3 chain from v1 reaches v3 and the 1-4 chain from v1 reaches v4, can actually occur, and then every single interchange fails.
counterexample: G: vertex v joined to v1,v2,v3,v4,v5; the 5-cycle v1v2v3v4v5; plus chords v1v3 (drawn outside, around v2) and v1v4 (drawn outside, around v5). G is planar and simple, and deg v = 5. Coloring c of G-v: v1=1, v2=2, v3=3, v4=4, v5=2. It is proper and uses all four colors on N(v). Every Kempe interchange: {1,2}: one component {v1,v2,v5} gives 2,1,3,4,1. {1,3}: {v1,v3} gives 3,2,1,4,2. {1,4}: {v1,v4} gives 4,2,3,1,2. {2,3}: components {v2,v3} gives 1,3,2,4,2, and {v5} gives 1,2,3,4,3. {2,4}: components {v4,v5} gives 1,2,3,2,4, and {v2} gives 1,4,3,4,2. {3,4}: {v3,v4} gives 1,2,4,3,2. All still use four colors.
assessment_summary:
Proof attempt, with a judgment on each step:
1. Name the neighbors v1..v5 in cyclic order. Exactly one color is repeated, so WLOG c = (1,2,3,4,2) on v1..v5. JUSTIFIED: 5 vertices and 4 colors, so exactly one repeat; relabel colors and rotate.
2. One swap leaves at most 3 colors only if it removes color 1, 3 or 4 from N(v), or removes 2 from both v2 and v5, without bringing in the missing color. JUSTIFIED: this just lists the ways the color count can drop.
3. Suppose (as in a near-triangulation) consecutive neighbors are adjacent. Then the 3-2 chain at v3 contains v2, the 4-2 chain at v4 contains v5, the 3-4 chains are joined, and the 1-2 chain at v2 contains v1. So these swaps cannot work. Only two swaps are left: the 1-3 swap at v1 when v3 is not in that chain, or the 1-4 swap at v1 when v4 is not in that chain. JUSTIFIED: follows from the adjacencies.
4. Claim: one of those two chain conditions must hold. NOT JUSTIFIED. Nothing stops both chains from connecting (Kempe's case). Kempe's own argument needed two simultaneous swaps here, which Heawood showed can fail. A concrete graph where both chains connect is G = W5 plus the outer chords v1v3 and v1v4, with c = (1,2,3,4,2). Checking all six color pairs and every component (see counterexample) shows no single interchange reduces N(v) to three colors.
5. Conclusion that c extends after one interchange. NOT JUSTIFIED: it depends on step 4.
The statement claims this for every planar G and every such coloring, so the explicit counterexample shows it is false. (G itself is 4-colorable, but not by one Kempe interchange from c.)
